title: Quadratic forms and positive definiteness
terms: quadratic form; positive definite matrix; positive semidefinite matrix; Sylvester criterion; Sylvester law of inertia.

exposition.text:
T
A real quadratic form has the shape q(x) = x Ax, where A may be taken symmetric because
the skew-symmetric part contributes zero. It is positive definite if q(x) > 0 for every nonzero x,
and positive semidefinite if q(x) ≥ 0 for all x. By the spectral theorem, these conditions mean
respectively that all eigenvalues of A are positive or nonnegative.
Sylvester’s criterion tests positive definiteness of a real symmetric matrix by positivity of all
leading principal minors. For semidefiniteness one must check all principal minors, not merely
the leading ones. Orthogonal diagonalization turns the quadratic form into a sum of eigenval-
ues times squared coordinates. On the unit sphere its extrema are the extreme eigenvalues;
constraints may change the relevant subspace.
Sylvester's law of inertia says that an invertible real linear change of variables preserves the
numbers of positive, negative, and zero squares in a diagonalized real quadratic form. Such
T
a change acts by congruence A 7→ P AP; it need not preserve the individual eigenvalues. A
principal minor uses the same subset of row and column indices; a leading principal minor uses
the first k indices.

question.text:
A real symmetric matrix has all its leading principal minors nonnegative. Which conclusion is
justified?
(A) It is positive definite.
(B) It is positive semidefinite.
(C) It is nonsingular.
(D) No semidefiniteness conclusion follows; diag(0, −1) is a counterexample.
(E) It has no negative eigenvalues.

solution.text:
2
The leading minors of diag(0, −1) are both zero, but its quadratic form is −y , which is
negative for (0, 1). For positive semidefiniteness, all principal minors must be nonnegative,
including the lower-right one-by-one minor. The strictly positive leading-minor criterion for
positive definiteness cannot simply be weakened to nonnegative leading minors.

question.text:
How many positive and negative squares occur in a diagonalization by real invertible change of
2 2 2
variables of x + 4xy + y − z ?
(A) Two positive and one negative
(B) One positive and two negative
(C) Three positive and none negative
(D) None positive and three negative
(E) One positive, one negative, and one zero

solution.text:
The x, y block has eigenvalues 3 and −1, while the z coefficient is −1. Sylvester’s law of
inertia preserves these sign counts under invertible changes of variables, giving one positive
and two negative squares.
